title: Chapter 15: Testing, Debugging, and Logging
description: Create layered evidence for correctness and diagnosis. Learners design deterministic unit, integration, and journey tests; use JUnit assertions and parameterized cases; choose fakes or mocks at genuine boundaries; debug from a minimal reproduction and explicit hypothesis; and design logs, metrics, and traces that distinguish failures without duplicating noise or leaking secrets.

lessons.title: Test pyramid, boundaries, determinism, and test naming
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Test pyramid, boundaries, determinism, and test naming

## Tests answer different questions
A unit test exercises a small behavior quickly. An integration test verifies a real boundary such as SQL mapping or filesystem behavior. An end-to-end test checks a user journey across components. More expensive tests should cover critical interactions rather than duplicate every unit case.

```java
static void check(boolean condition, String message) {
    if (!condition) throw new AssertionError(message);
}
check(rectangleArea(3, 4) == 12, "area of 3 by 4");
```
This plain-Java assertion helper runs without dependencies. Java's built-in assert statement is disabled by default unless enabled, so it is not an unconditional production validation mechanism.

## Test selection
Partition inputs into meaningful classes and test their boundaries: below, equal, and above a threshold. Include failure paths and unchanged-state assertions. A test that only repeats the implementation's formula may share its mistake; use independently reasoned expected values.

## Practice
Write a test matrix for withdrawals covering negative, zero, allowed, exact-balance, and excessive amounts. Inject a fixed clock for time-dependent behavior. Run tests in another order to expose shared mutable fixtures. Coverage numbers identify unexecuted code but do not prove useful assertions.

exercises.instructionMarkdown: What does line coverage fail to prove?
choices: That assertions test the right behavior
hints: Coverage tools only record that a line executed; they cannot tell you whether the assertions that ran actually validate the right behavior.

lessons.title: Fakes, stubs, spies, mocks, and Mockito judgment
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Fakes, stubs, spies, mocks, and Mockito judgment

## Test doubles serve different roles
A stub returns controlled answers. A fake is a simplified working implementation, such as an in-memory repository. A mock verifies selected interactions. A spy wraps real behavior while observing or replacing some calls.

```java
final class RecordingSink implements ReceiptSink {
    final java.util.List<String> messages = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
    public void write(String text) { messages.add(text); }
}
```
This fake records outputs without a mocking library. Use it to assert the receipt contract. Mockito can stub and verify interface interactions in an external test project, but it does not make a test meaningful automatically.

## Avoid brittle tests
Mocking every object couples tests to private call sequences and makes harmless refactoring fail. Prefer value assertions for domain rules, fakes for stable ports, and integration tests for database or framework behavior. A mock JDBC connection does not prove the SQL is valid.

## Practice
Test Checkout with RecordingSink, then simulate a failing sink. Define whether payment state changes when output fails. Verify only interactions that are part of the contract, such as preventing a duplicate charge. Explain what remains untested by the fake.

exercises.instructionMarkdown: Does a mock JDBC connection prove SQL correctness?

hints: A mocked Connection only returns whatever stubbed answers you configure; it never actually parses or executes SQL against a real schema.

lessons.title: Reproduction, hypotheses, breakpoints, stepping, and thread dumps
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Reproduction, hypotheses, breakpoints, stepping, and thread dumps

## Distinguish symptom and cause
Start with the smallest reproducing input and expected behavior. Form a hypothesis that can be disproved by one observation. If a sorted result is wrong, inspect the comparator before changing storage or adding logging everywhere.

```java
int[] values = {2, 4};
int total = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < values.length - 1; i++) total += values[i];
// Expected 6, actual 2: inspect the final loop condition.
```
A breakpoint on the loop lets you inspect i and total. Conditional breakpoints pause only for a chosen input. Watch expressions may invoke methods and cause side effects; inspect carefully.

## Threads and stacks
A thread dump shows where threads are running, waiting, or blocked. Several blocked threads are not automatically a deadlock; look for a cycle of held and requested locks. Stack traces locate failure paths, while heap evidence helps retained-memory problems.

## Practice
Write the hypothesis “the final element is skipped,” verify it, and make the smallest fix. Keep a regression test for a singleton array, where this bug returns zero. Document a failed hypothesis as well as the successful one so the reasoning is reproducible.

exercises.title: Reproduction, hypotheses, breakpoints, stepping, and thread dumps: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: What is a useful debugging hypothesis?
choices: A conclusion based only on compilation
A specific explanation that an observation can disprove
A random edit that might help
hints: A useful hypothesis names a specific mechanism, such as an off-by-one loop bound, that a single targeted observation could prove false.

lessons.title: Structured logging, levels, correlation, metrics, and traces
lessons.theoryMarkdown:
# Structured logging, levels, correlation, metrics, and traces

## Record events with useful context
```java
var logger = java.util.logging.Logger.getLogger("academy.orders");
logger.log(java.util.logging.Level.INFO,
    "Order completed: id={0}, items={1}", new Object[] {orderId, itemCount});
```
The standard logger needs no external library. SLF4J and implementations such as Logback require declared dependencies; select an abstraction and backend deliberately. Include stable event names and correlation identifiers, and retain throwable objects when logging failures.

## Logs, metrics, traces
Logs describe individual events. Metrics aggregate counts and distributions. Traces connect spans across a request path. Do not place user IDs or unbounded URLs into metric labels: cardinality can overwhelm storage. Never log credentials, tokens, or unnecessary personal data.

Log an exception once at the boundary that owns its response; lower layers should preserve context through causes rather than duplicate the same stack trace.

## Practice
Design events for task_created, task_rejected, and storage_unavailable. Define severity and safe fields. Trace a failed request from correlation ID to the cause. Add a duration metric using a monotonic time source and explain why wall-clock adjustments can invalidate elapsed-time calculations.

exercises.title: Structured logging, levels, correlation, metrics, and traces: concept check
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Why avoid user IDs as metric labels?
choices: Unbounded cardinality can overload metric storage
Metric labels are limited to a single fixed value at compile time
High-cardinality labels only affect log file size, not the metrics backend
hints: Each distinct label value creates a new time series in most metrics backends, so unbounded values like user IDs can multiply storage and query cost.

# Chapter 15 assessment

Before touching the debugger, use this chapter's rules on Java's disabled-by-default assert statement to predict what **An assertion must execute without JVM flags** should print, then run it and repair the defect so the check fails without relying on the -ea flag.

The diagnostic function lab exercises one formatting contract in isolation; it is not proof of every competency from test design through structured logging covered across the chapter's five lessons. Review the repaired source and explain why assert alone cannot be trusted for this check, without consulting the answer.

exercises.title: Chapter 15 implementation lab: diagnostic
exercises.instructionMarkdown:
Implement `diagnostic`. Return exactly expected=<expected>, actual=<actual> using the two integer values. Write the precondition and boundary table first, keep the method deterministic, and do not print.

Use the exact punctuation shown; no extra whitespace or line endings.
hints: Match the exact literal text 'expected=' and ', actual=' with no extra spaces or punctuation.
Check zero and negative values for both parameters before submitting, since the format must hold for every integer.

exercises.title: An assertion must execute without JVM flags
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Repair the check so it does not rely on Java's disabled-by-default assert statement, and the program writes exactly `true`. Keep the same failed-flag pattern and explain why assert silently does nothing without the -ea flag while an explicit throw does not, rather than hard-coding the print statement. Output tests verify the printed result; confirming the check truly executes requires reading the source.
hints: Replace the disabled-by-default assert statement with an explicit check that throws AssertionError.

exercises.title: Validated monthly expense report
exercises.instructionMarkdown: Implement MonthlyReport.run(String input). Each nonblank line contains date|cents. Trim fields. Date must have ASCII yyyy-MM-dd shape and be a valid LocalDate in years 0001..9999; cents must be a positive int. Reject bad records and count ERRORS. Group accepted amounts by YearMonth and sum into long. Output months in ascending order as yyyy-MM=total, followed by ERRORS=<count>. Empty input returns ERRORS=0. Use explicit parsing, preserve valid records after errors, and do not use the real current date. At most 10000 input lines are supplied; this bounds total amounts.
hints: Parse and validate all fields before mutating state. Split with a negative limit when empty fields must be preserved.
Choose collections according to identity and ordering requirements. Build output lines and join them with a newline.
